slide.title: Measure, Don't Trust
slide.body: Two text-on-background swatches with a contrast readout: bright saffron on white marked fail, darker saffron on white marked pass. Small tag: AI for Brand and Product Design · Lesson 9.

scenes.voiceover: Claude suggests a beautiful palette, and writes: these colours have good contrast. Do they? The only way to know is to measure.

slide.title: Colour, Type and Accessible Brand Systems
slide.body: AI for Brand and Product Design · Lesson 9 of 14

scenes.voiceover: Last time, we redrew a logo by hand. Now we turn it into a brand system. This lesson is about colour, type and accessible brand systems.

slide.title: Ask for roles and reasons
slide.body:
Suggest 3 palettes of 5 colours each, with hex codes, for a brand that feels trustworthy and warm. For each colour, give its role (primary, secondary, background, text, accent) and one reason.

Suggest 3 type pairings, one for headings and one for body text, that are free to use and support Latin and Arabic scripts.

scenes.voiceover: Claude can help here, because it can suggest options with reasons linked to your brief. For example, ask for three palettes of five colours, with hex codes, a role for each colour, and one reason. For type, ask for pairings that are free to use and support the scripts you need, such as Latin and Arabic.

slide.title: What can go wrong
slide.body: Hex codes that do not match the described colour · Contrast claims that were never calculated · Fonts that do not exist or lack your scripts

scenes.voiceover: Treat these suggestions as a starting point. Language models can give hex codes that do not match the colour they describe. They can claim contrast values without calculating them. And they can suggest fonts that do not exist, or that do not support your scripts. So you test everything yourself.

slide.title: Test every text pair
slide.body: Text swatch on background swatch → contrast checker → ratio and pass/fail at level AA (body text and large text shown separately)

scenes.voiceover: First, test colour contrast. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, or WCAG, set minimum contrast ratios between text and background, with a higher minimum for normal body text than for large text. Test every text and background pair you plan to use, with a contrast checker plugin in Figma or a free web checker.

scenes.on_screen_text: Fails? Adjust it. Keep the original decorative.
scenes.voiceover: If a pair fails, darken or lighten one colour until it passes. Then keep the original colour for decoration only.

slide.title: Test type in real conditions
slide.body: Body text at 12–14 px: are I, l and 1 clear? · Real words in Arabic and Devanagari, not only Latin · Balanced weights · Line height for taller scripts · A reader of the script checks it

scenes.voiceover: Next, test type in real conditions. Set body text at small sizes, like twelve to fourteen pixels, and check that a capital I, a small l and the number one are clear. If your brand uses other scripts, such as Arabic or Devanagari, test real words in those scripts. Check the weights, the line height, and ask a reader of that script to review it.

scenes.stock_query: person holding paint swatches against wall
scenes.on_screen_text: Test it on your own wall
scenes.voiceover: Think of an AI palette as a paint chart from a shop. The colours look good on the card, but you still test them on your own wall, in your own light, before you paint the whole room.

Let's measure a real palette. Omar Haddad is a product designer in Amman, Jordan. His client is a money-transfer app for workers who send money between Jordan and Nepal. The brand must work in English, Arabic and Nepali, which uses the Devanagari script.

slide.title: Claude's palette
slide.body: Five swatches: navy #1E3A5F · saffron #E07A3F · cream #F6F1E7 · green #2E8B57 · warm grey #9A8F80. Speech bubble: 'All colours work well for text.' with a question mark

scenes.voiceover: Claude suggests five colours: navy, saffron, cream, green and warm grey. It says that all of them work well for text. Omar does not accept that. He tests each text pair he plans to use.

slide.title: Contrast results
slide.body: Navy on cream 10.22:1 Pass · Saffron on white 2.99:1 Fail · Green on white 4.25:1 Fail · Warm grey on cream 2.82:1 Fail · Saffron on navy 3.85:1 Large text only

scenes.voiceover: Navy on cream measures ten point two two to one, and passes. But saffron on white measures only two point nine nine to one. Green on white and warm grey on cream also fail for body text. Saffron on navy works for large text only.

slide.title: Fixing the failures
slide.body: Saffron #E07A3F (2.99:1) → #B8561F (4.78:1 on white) for text and buttons; bright saffron kept for illustrations · Green → #1F6B45 (6.47:1) · Warm grey → #6B6154 (5.39:1 on cream)

scenes.voiceover: So he fixes the failures. He darkens saffron for text and buttons, and it now measures four point seven eight to one on white. He keeps the brighter saffron for illustrations. He also darkens the green and the warm grey until both pass.

slide.title: Type in three scripts
slide.body: Red cross: suggested pairing without Devanagari. Green tick: one free family with Latin, Arabic and Devanagari; a transfer amount and a short message at 14 px in all three scripts; reviewed by readers of Arabic and Nepali

scenes.voiceover: For type, Claude suggested a pairing where one font had no Devanagari support. Omar chooses a free font family with Latin, Arabic and Devanagari versions. He tests transfer amounts and short messages at fourteen pixels in all three scripts, and asks two colleagues who read Arabic and Nepali to check the text.

scenes.on_screen_text: Test every pair you will use.
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to accept an AI statement like this palette is accessible, without measuring. Another is to test only the main brand colour on white, and forget grey helper text, button text or text on coloured cards. List every pair you will use, and test each one.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. AI suggestions are unverified: hex codes, fonts, contrast claims. 2. Test every text pair against WCAG; adjust to fix. 3. Test type small and in every script, with real readers.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, use Claude to suggest palettes and type pairings with roles and reasons, but treat every hex code, font and contrast claim as unverified. Second, test every text and background pair against WCAG contrast guidance, and fix failures by adjusting the colour. Third, test type at small sizes and in every script your brand needs, with real readers.

scenes.on_screen_text: Next: Building Brand Guidelines in Figma
scenes.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will build a palette of five colours and a type pairing for your brand, test all text colour pairs for contrast, and fix any that fail. It takes about thirty-five minutes. In the next lesson, we build brand guidelines in Figma. See you there.
